question.note: Regional and event-driven variation in the US and Canada across the three topics (Q1). The methods aim (Q2) is only in the quote, not the claim.
Only the vaccination correlate of Q3; ideological leaning and conspiracy content not named.

flags.text: Frames the question as whether events 'cause' spikes; the paper says spikes are 'linked to' events and 'direct causal evidence is not available' (p.17).

question.note: Event-driven variation, Q1's temporal half (repeat of Q1). Spikes are presupposed, not reported as a finding, so no misplaced F3.

central_claim.note: Abstract wording ('significantly higher ... in both countries'), credited per C1's decision. No B1 catch.
US vaccination correlation (F2's US half) placed in central_claim. 'Tangible public health implications' is the abstract's wording; not flagged.
Short-lived event-linked spikes: the finding F3, placed here.

evidence.note: Over 50 million tweets with exact dates (Oct 9, 2020 to Jan 4, 2021) and keyword/topic filtering; the US/Canada split is not given, treated as detail.
Geocoding tools named but not that locations come from the profile location field (partial E4); two-step profile/activity classifier without the external validation (partial E3).
Validation against election results and voter records: the validation half of E3.
Keyword lists for the initial filter (p.5). Accurate method detail; the asymmetry is not stated as a limit here, so no L4.
Four topics including conspiracy, hashtag annotation and fine-tuned domain-adapted RoBERTa.
Subsampling approximation of the polarization index (p.11). Accurate; not in the gold.
Vaccination rates one year after the tweets; election and case data not named.
Canadian parties merged into two families because the classifier confused them (p.8). The method behind L8, stated as method, not as a limit (as the earlier judge decided).
Voter-registration validation (30,000+ users, 74.35% / 73.35%; p.8-10): validation half of E3.
OSM/ArcGIS agreement within one degree (p.6); still does not say the input is the profile location field, so E4 is not completed or joined.

key_findings.note: US half of F1 (masks and vaccines higher, lockdowns mixed); Canada's non-significance not stated. Delaware and Idaho named as outliers without direction: part of F6.

Events (Trump lockdown tweets, Biden's vaccination; Tables 9 and p.18) tied to spikes; that spikes last only days is not stated. 'Triggered' echoes the paper's 'event-triggered' wording (p.21); not flagged.

Conservatives tweet conspiracy content at higher rates ('tweeted', not 'endorsed', so not F-x3) plus the US small negative / Canada no correlation. Quote covers only the US correlation; still in the paper.
Canada lower overall (F5's first half; the weaker association with conservatism not stated). Quebec highest with the English-only caveat (F7).
Appended entry. Event-triggered spikes lasting a few days with rise-and-decay (p.1, p.19).

flags.text: Says users from the liberal party family retweeted American vaccine content eight times more than Canadian content; the paper says 'Canadians' did so, citing refs 94 and 95 (p.24), with no party breakdown.

key_findings.note: Appended entry. Also a cited result, not this paper's finding.

Appended entry. Aggregate polarization not correlated with pandemic severity (S6 Fig caption, p.27). Accurate; not in the gold.

scope_and_limits.note: Suggestive, not causal, because of the time gap (L5). 'Complexity of social factors' and the quote gesture at L6, but the claim limits it to the vaccination correlation.
Self-reported locations, VPNs and bots; the possible inflation of partisan distance not stated.
Semantic-similarity proxy may miss signals; sarcasm example left out (detail).
Duplicates part of entry 2, with dates.
Bots may inflate apparent semantic distance: the second half of L3. With entry 3 (self-reported locations, VPNs, bots) the note states all of L3.

theoretical_positioning.note: Text-embedding approach chosen over network-based methods. No T0.

Group-specific lexicons make topic conditioning necessary (p.4): the prior-work claim I7 that the method handles, placed here (as the earlier judge did). 'Stronger proxy' follows the paper's 'more likely reflects'; not flagged.
Adds geographic and event-driven resolution; does not say it agrees with earlier findings on right-leaning regions.

interlocutor_claim.note: The topic-conditioning point (p.4). The prior-work claim that groups have their own lexicon is in the quote, not the claim, and 'disputes the assumption' attributes the naive view to no one; the paper's own wording rejects it ('does not necessarily indicate'), so not flagged.
Builds on and extends prior work (p.22), but the prior claim is given only as 'partisan divergence in pandemic response', not that right-leaning states were more divided.
Owen et al. (correct for ref. 94): reduced negative sentiment in 2020, contrasted with the paper's Canadian result.
Delaware high; Arkansas, Alabama, Idaho low (p.23): F6, framed as disputing a generalization attributed to no one. The paper itself says the pattern 'was not universal'; not flagged.
